title: Model-Agnostic Random Weighting for Out-of-Distribution Generalization

problem.claim: Machine learning methods based on the i.i.d. assumption can suffer performance deterioration under training-test distribution shift.

gap.claim: A particularly challenging OOD setting is improving generalization when training data come from only a single environment.

contributions.claim: A model-agnostic method addresses the single-environment OOD setting by pursuing robust weighted empirical risks using randomly shifted training distributions generated through sample-based weighting.
The expected risk under the shifted training distribution is theoretically established to bound the expected risk under the test distribution.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors state that the theoretical foundation ensures improved prediction performance under uncertain test distributions.
The authors report extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets affirming the method's effectiveness for distribution-shift problems.

narrative_sequence.summary: Distribution shift can degrade methods built on the i.i.d. assumption, motivating OOD generalization research.
The paper focuses on OOD generalization from samples drawn from a single environment.
The proposed approach uses model-agnostic robust weighted empirical risks and randomly shifted training distributions based on sample weighting.
A risk bound supports the approach, and experiments on diverse real-world datasets are reported as evidence of effectiveness.

source_observation.claim: Random sample-based weighting is used to create shifted training distributions and optimize robust weighted empirical risks.

interpretation.claim: Training against a controlled family of weighted shifts may improve robustness when the deployment distribution is uncertain.

application.claim: A model-agnostic weighting strategy could be considered for single-environment training scenarios with anticipated distribution shift.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify whether the approach applies equally well when multiple training environments or known shift structure are available.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the sample-weighting procedure or training algorithm.
The assumptions and exact form of the theoretical risk bound are unspecified.
Datasets, baselines, metrics, and quantitative experimental results are not provided.
